bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Jungheinrich's earnings collapse was mostly an accounting event, not a business event, and that the market has repriced the whole company as if it were the latter. Jungheinrich is the number-two maker of forklift trucks and warehouse equipment in Europe, family-controlled, based in Hamburg. Its revenue has been flat at roughly 5.5 billion euros for three straight years (5.55bn in 2023, 5.39bn in 2024, 5.50bn in 2025) through one of the worst European industrial capital-spending stretches in a decade. Over the same period the share price has fallen from about 38 euros to 24.32 euros, and reported earnings per share fell 64%, from 2.83 euros in 2024 to 1.02 euros in 2025.

Take that collapse apart and it does not look like a broken business. Operating profit fell 19%, from 441 million to 358 million euros, which is an ordinary cyclical result. What turned a 19% operating decline into a 64% earnings decline was roughly 162 million euros of charges booked below the operating line (against 21 million the year before) and an effective tax rate of 47% on the profit that survived. Both trace back to the planned disposal of the Russian business. Strip those out and the underlying earning power of this company is far closer to the 2.80-3.00 euros a share it produced in 2023 and 2024 than to the 1.02 euros the screen shows.

The most important corroborating number is the one that did not move: gross margin, which has held at 32.2%. If Jungheinrich were losing a competitive fight to KION or to Toyota Industries, the damage would appear there first. It has not appeared. What has happened instead is that a flat revenue line stopped covering a fixed cost base, which is operating leverage working in reverse - painful, cyclical, and reversible.

The leading indicator has already turned. In the half-year report published on 11 August 2026, second-quarter order intake beat expectations, led by warehouse equipment. Orders turn before revenue, and revenue turns before margin, so this is the correct sequence for a recovery that has begun. The analysts who read the half-year detail became more constructive rather than less: Citi upgraded to buy on 14 August 2026 with a 32-euro target, and Bernstein raised its target to 47 euros on 19 August 2026. Consensus across eleven analysts sits at about 35.45 euros, roughly 46% above the current price, and consensus models a return to a 7.7% operating margin and 2.96 euros of earnings per share by 2027.

The balance sheet gives the thesis time to work. At 30 June 2026 the company held 723 million euros of cash and short-term investments against 701 million of total debt - a small net cash position - with shareholders' equity of 2,556 million euros, or 25.06 euros a share. The stock trades at 0.97 times book value with no debt maturity wall, and the share count has been unchanged at 102 million for six years, so there has been no dilution. Enterprise value is about 3.6 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.

Structurally, this is a company on the right side of its industry's secular force rather than the wrong side. Warehouse automation is the change reshaping material handling, and Jungheinrich sells automated guided vehicles, warehouse robotics and racking, and bought the American automation business Storage Solutions in 2023 for roughly 330 million euros precisely to be there. E-commerce increases the demand for warehouse equipment; it does not destroy it. Electrification is a tailwind for a company that led on lithium-ion trucks. There is no melting terminal value underneath this multiple.

Conditions the bull case depends on: (1) the regulator's examination of the June 2025 accounts closes without a finding of error; (2) the operating margin troughs in the first half of 2026 at 6.2% and recovers toward 7.5% over the next four to six quarters, which the 10 November 2026 nine-month statement is the first chance to evidence; (3) the effective tax rate normalises from 45% back toward the German statutory 30% once the Russian losses are behind the group; and (4) European warehouse and industrial capital spending does not take a second leg down.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that this is a fairly-priced, low-return industrial with an unresolved accounting problem, and that almost everything that makes it look cheap on a screen is an artefact.

Start with the free-cash-flow figure that drives the screen. Jungheinrich reported 346 million euros of free cash flow in 2025, which against a 2.48 billion euro market value produces a 12% free-cash yield and a 7.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple. But capital expenditure of 145 million euros is only 0.30 times depreciation of 479 million. No company can depreciate 479 million euros of assets a year while replacing 145 million of them. The missing spend is the short-term rental and lease fleet, which does not sit in that capital-expenditure line. The headline cash generation, and the cheap multiple built on top of it, overstate what this business actually produces after keeping its fleet current. Anyone underwriting a 12% free-cash yield here is underwriting a classification, not a cash flow.

Second, the recovery has not started in the numbers that matter. First-half 2026 revenue was 2,669 million euros against 2,657 million a year earlier - up 0.5%, which is less than inflation. Operating profit fell 21%, from 211 million to 166 million euros. The operating margin of 6.2% is below 2025's full-year 6.5% and well below 2024's 8.2%. Earnings per share halved again, from 1.37 euros to 0.72. Three consecutive reporting periods of margin compression is a trend, not a trough. The order beat reported on 11 August 2026 is genuine but it is one quarter, and the market's reaction to it - shares closed flat - says the market has stopped paying for order intake in this name.

Third, and most seriously, the German financial regulator BaFin opened an examination of Jungheinrich's financial statements as at 30 June 2025 on 21 July 2026, connected to the planned disposal of the Russian business. That is the exact accounting - the disposal charges - that produced both the earnings collapse and the punitive 47% tax rate the bull case wants to dismiss as one-off. Under German enforcement practice a finding of error must be published, and there is no announced timetable. If the finding goes against the company, it arrives as an unscheduled headline into a stock already down about 36% from its 52-week high, and the 'one-off charges' framing that the entire normalised-earnings argument rests on goes with it. This risk cannot be handicapped from public information and cannot be hedged by waiting for a date, because there is no date.

Fourth, management's own confidence broke this summer. On 23 July 2026 the company cut its 2026 forecast, four months after setting it at the March balance-sheet press conference, and the shares fell more than 5%. DZ Bank cut its fair value from 43 to 35 euros the same day. Our tracking shows the company has beaten expectations in only two of the last five quarters. This is not a sandbagging management team whose guidance can be trusted as a floor; it is one that has been too optimistic and had to retreat.

Fifth, the effective tax rate is a structural wedge between an operating recovery and an earnings recovery. At 47% in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026 against a German statutory rate near 30%, the arithmetic says there are losses in the group that cannot be sheltered. Even if operating profit returns fully to 440 million euros, a 45% tax rate rather than a normal 30% costs roughly 0.60 euros of earnings per share. Consensus earnings of 2.96 euros for 2027 implicitly assume this normalises. If it does not, the forward multiple people think they are paying is meaningfully wrong.

Sixth, this is not a high-return business even at the top of its cycle. The best operating margin Jungheinrich has ever produced is around 8.5%. Return on invested capital today is 5.8% and return on equity 11.5%. A narrow-moat industrial that earns single-digit returns on capital does not deserve a premium multiple, and at 0.97 times book with a mid-cycle recovery already the consensus base case, it is not obviously getting a discount either.

Seventh, there is no lever. The listed instrument is the non-voting preference share; the ordinary shares are held by the founding family and are not listed. No activist can force a break-up, a buyback, a sale or a board change. Every classic special-situation escape route is structurally closed. The only thing that fixes this stock is the company earning its way out, on its own timetable.

Finally, the dividend looks stretched. The company paid 80.5 million euros against 103.6 million of earnings in 2025 - a 78% payout at a cyclical trough - and first-half 2026 earnings of 0.72 euros a share do not comfortably support holding it flat. A cut announced with the full-year results in late March 2027 would be the correct capital-allocation decision and would still force German income-oriented funds to sell mechanically.

What would confirm the bear case: a nine-month operating margin below 6.5% on 10 November 2026; a second guidance cut in the same statement; any BaFin finding of error; or an effective tax rate still above 40% in the full-year 2026 accounts.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is narrower than usual, and it is worth being honest about that up front: there is no hidden view available in this name. Eleven analysts cover it, all of them are positive, consensus sits at about 35.45 euros - roughly 46% above the 24.32 euro price - and the sell side got more constructive after reading the half-year detail, with Citi upgrading to buy on 14 August 2026 and Bernstein raising its target to 47 euros on 19 August 2026. This is a fully-covered, fully-liked German mid-cap. There is no under-coverage edge to harvest.

Our disagreement is with the pace, not the direction, and it rests on two specific street assumptions we think are factually wrong.

First, consensus models a 7.7% operating margin and 2.96 euros of earnings per share for 2027, rising to 3.29 euros in 2028 - which is essentially a full return to the 2023-24 structure within eighteen months. But the first half of 2026 delivered a 6.2% margin, which is lower than 2025's full-year 6.5% and lower again than 2024's 8.2%. Three consecutive reporting periods of compression on flat revenue is not the shape of a business one quarter from recovery. We model 7.25% as the normalised level - half a point below the street - and we do not think that half point is conservatism, we think it is the difference between a company that has recovered operating leverage and one that has merely stopped losing it.

Second, and more consequential, the street is treating the effective tax rate as transitory. Jungheinrich paid 47% in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026 against a German statutory rate near 30%. Two consecutive periods at that level is not noise - it is the signature of losses in subsidiaries that cannot be sheltered and charges that cannot be deducted, which is precisely what a Russian disposal produces. A consensus earnings figure of 2.96 euros for 2027 requires the tax rate to normalise. If it does not, the arithmetic costs roughly 0.60 euros a share even on a full operating recovery, and the forward multiple the market thinks it is paying is materially wrong. Nobody in the published analyst record appears to be pressing on this.

There is a third point on which we think the screening community, rather than the analyst community, is wrong. The stock screens at 7.3 times price to free cash flow with a 12% free-cash yield. Capital expenditure of 145 million euros is 0.30 times depreciation of 479 million. A company cannot depreciate 479 million euros of assets while replacing 145 million of them; the missing spend is the short-term rental and lease fleet, which does not sit in that line. The cheap cash-flow multiple is a classification artefact, and it is the single most quoted reason to own this stock. That correction cuts against the bulls, and it is the reason our base-case fair value of 28.94 euros sits well below the 35.45 euro consensus target rather than above it.

Net: the market is not looking the wrong way here. It is looking the right way, slightly too early, on cash flow that is slightly overstated, with a tax assumption nobody has stress-tested.
forcing_function:
There is no clean forcing event here, and saying otherwise would be inventing one. What exists is two dated reporting checkpoints and one undated regulatory resolution.

The first dated checkpoint is the nine-month interim statement on 10 November 2026, taken from the company's published financial calendar. This is the first opportunity to evidence that the 6.2% first-half operating margin was the trough. A margin back above 7.0% with the second-quarter order momentum sustained would begin the re-rating; anything below 6.5%, or a second guidance cut, ends the debate the other way.

The second dated checkpoint is the full-year 2026 results and the 2027 guide, delivered at the balance-sheet press conference in late March 2027 (the 2026 equivalent was held on 27 March). This is where three things resolve at once: whether the effective tax rate normalises from 45% toward the statutory 30%, whether the dividend is cut, and what management commits to for 2027 against the 7.7% operating margin consensus already assumes.

The undated item is the German regulator's examination of the 30 June 2025 accounts, opened 21 July 2026. Its conclusion is the single largest binary in this file and it has no timetable. A clean close would remove the accounting cloud and is, in our view, worth several euros a share on its own, because it would validate the 'one-off charges' framing that the normalised-earnings case depends on. A finding of error would do the reverse.

What is deliberately absent from this list: any buyback authorisation, activist campaign, asset sale or strategic process. The non-voting share structure and family control make all of those unavailable, so the usual deep-value forcing functions simply do not apply to this name. This company can only earn its way out.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has three specific hazards. Note first what is not a hazard: there is no cash-burn problem and no maturity wall. At 30 June 2026 the company held 723 million euros of cash and short-term investments against 701 million euros of total debt, and it has not diluted shareholders in six years. The risk in this name is earnings and headlines, not solvency. The 2.0 Altman-Z solvency reading on our screen is depressed by the captive leasing book sitting inside the group balance sheet; the industrial company itself is financed conservatively.

Hazard one, and the largest: the German regulator's open examination of the 30 June 2025 accounts, opened 21 July 2026 and connected to the planned Russian disposal. Under German enforcement practice a finding of error must be published, and there is no announced timetable - it could land next month or next year. If it lands badly it arrives as an unscheduled headline into a share already about 36% below its 52-week high of 38.16 euros, and it destroys the 'these were one-off charges' framing on which the entire normalised-earnings argument depends. This cannot be handicapped from public information and cannot be waited out to a date, because there is no date. It is the reason we will not size this name at any price without either the file closing or a much larger discount.

Hazard two: the nine-month interim statement on 10 November 2026. The first-half operating margin was 6.2%. A third consecutive period below 7% would confirm the bear reading that this is the new normal rather than a trough, and would very likely take the shares through the 21.72 euro 52-week low. Worse, the company already cut its 2026 forecast once, on 23 July 2026, four months after setting it - a second cut in the November statement is a live possibility and would be far more damaging than the first, because the first can be excused as macro and the second cannot.

Hazard three: the tax line keeps doing damage even if trading improves. At a 45% effective rate, an operating recovery does not become an earnings recovery. The full-year 2026 accounts, published in late March 2027, are where this either normalises or is revealed as structural.

One further point on timing. The share has been going nowhere for two months - the 50-day average is 24.34 euros against a 24.32 euro price - which means there is no momentum working for a buyer and no urgency to commit. Waiting costs almost nothing here.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling picture has one clear source and one structural blocker.

The source is the dividend. Jungheinrich paid 80.5 million euros to shareholders in respect of 2025 against 103.6 million euros of earnings - a 78% payout ratio struck at a cyclical trough - and that payment has already been made, on 22 May 2026, so there is no pending distribution left to collect. First-half 2026 earnings of 0.72 euros a share do not comfortably support holding the payout flat for a second year. A dividend cut announced alongside the full-year results in late March 2027 would be the correct capital-allocation decision and would still trigger mechanical selling: German mid-cap income funds and dividend-screened passive products hold this share for the yield, and a cut removes them from the register regardless of what they think of the recovery. That is the specific flush worth waiting for, and it has a date attached - the late-March 2027 balance-sheet press conference.

The structural blocker is the share class. The listed instrument is the non-voting preference share; the ordinary shares are held by the founding family and are not listed - which is why the freely-traded value of this company is only about 1.19 billion euros even though all 102 million shares at 24.32 euros are worth 2.48 billion. That structure means no activist can force a break-up, a buyback, a strategic review or a board change, and no takeover premium is available. Every classic special-situation lever - the governance reset, the pressured strategic process, the premium scenario - is structurally closed here. Any thesis that quietly assumes somebody will eventually act on the sum-of-the-parts discount is unsupported by the facts of the share register.

On current positioning: the share sits about 17% below its 200-day average of 29.37 euros and 17% up from its 52-week low, in a 21.72-38.16 range. Our smart-money reading is 8 out of 100 and institutional flow is neutral at 50 out of 100, and the insider buy ratio is zero - nobody inside the company has been buying this decline. For a family-controlled business whose owners have every informational advantage, an absence of insider buying at 0.97 times book is a data point worth registering.
moderator_conclusion:
Our call is to wait for a better price rather than buy here, at a moderate level of conviction, and to say plainly what we are waiting for.

The business case is more interesting than the screen suggests, and it is more interesting than the headline earnings collapse suggests. Jungheinrich's earnings per share fell 64% last year, from 2.83 euros to 1.02, but operating profit fell only 19%. Roughly two-thirds of that collapse came from about 162 million euros of charges booked below the operating line and an effective tax rate of 47%, both traceable to the planned disposal of the Russian business. Meanwhile gross margin has not moved at all - 32.2% and stable - which is the evidence that matters most, because a company losing a competitive fight loses it in gross margin first. Revenue has been flat rather than shrinking for three years through a poor European cycle, the balance sheet carries a small net cash position with no maturity wall, the share count has been unchanged for six years, and second-quarter order intake beat expectations in the half-year report published on 11 August 2026. This is a cyclically compressed, narrow-moat industrial - not a melting franchise. On the structural question the file reads well: warehouse automation is the force reshaping this industry and Jungheinrich sells into it rather than being displaced by it, e-commerce raises demand for warehouse equipment, and electrification is a tailwind for a company that led on lithium-ion trucks. The cheapness is a fear print, not a terminal decline.

Three things stop us buying it today.

The first is arithmetic. Our base-case sum-of-the-parts fair value is 28.94 euros a share, built from a normalised 7.25% operating margin on the industrial business at eight times operating profit, the captive leasing book at a modest premium to its estimated equity, and a small net cash overlay. Against a 24.32 euro price, that is a discount well short of what this book requires to commit capital, and the adverse case at 19.50 euros is almost exactly as far below the price as fair value is above it. Symmetric is not good enough.

The second is a correction to the reason most screens like this stock. It shows 7.3 times price to free cash flow and a 12% free-cash yield, but capital expenditure is running at 0.30 times depreciation - 145 million euros against 479 million. The short-term rental and lease fleet spend is not in that line. The cash-flow cheapness is a classification artefact, and correcting it is why our fair value sits below the 35.45 euro analyst consensus rather than above it. We also part company with consensus on tax: two consecutive periods at a 45%-plus effective rate against a 30% statutory rate is structural until proven otherwise, and it drives a wedge of roughly 0.60 euros a share between an operating recovery and an earnings recovery that the street's 2.96 euro 2027 estimate does not appear to carry.

The third is the regulator. On 21 July 2026 BaFin opened an examination of the 30 June 2025 financial statements in connection with the Russian disposal - which is to say, an examination of exactly the charges the bull case needs to be genuinely one-off. There is no timetable, a finding of error must be published, and the outcome cannot be handicapped from public information. Two days later, on 23 July, the company cut its own 2026 forecast four months after setting it. That is a poor pair of facts to buy into at a 16% discount.

We also note what this name does not offer. Eleven analysts cover it and every one is positive, so there is no coverage edge. The listed shares are non-voting preference shares with the ordinary shares held by the founding family, so no activist can force anything and no takeover premium exists - the usual deep-value escape hatches are structurally closed. And the discount to KION is largely the same European industrial capital-spending cycle both companies are riding, which makes it shared sector movement rather than company-specific edge; crediting it as edge would be double-counting.

So: what would change the call. Any one of three things. A price at or below 21.50 euros - through the 21.72 euro 52-week low - which would widen the discount to our fair value past 25% and clear the entry bar on the arithmetic alone. Or a nine-month operating margin back above 7.0% in the statement due 10 November 2026, confirming the first half was the trough and that the order beat is converting. Or the regulator closing its file without a finding of error, which would remove the one risk in this name we cannot price. The most likely flush, and the one we would most like to buy into, is a dividend cut announced with the full-year results in late March 2027: the payout was 78% of earnings at the trough, it is not comfortably affordable on current earnings, and cutting it would push the yield-oriented German fund holders out mechanically at exactly the moment the operating recovery becomes visible.

On the value case judged on its own - price against our fair value and the quality of the numbers, setting aside timing entirely - we rate it moderate. The discount is real but modest, the business is durable but narrow-moated and currently earning single-digit returns on capital, and there are three separate forensic amber lights: an open regulatory file, an unexplained tax rate, and a flattered cash-flow line. That is not a profile that earns a large position. It is a good name to own considerably lower, and the calendar gives us two dated chances - November and late March - to find out whether we will get it there.
sop_breakdown:
Base-case sum-of-the-parts of 28.94 euros a share, built from three pieces plus one overlay. This is a functional split inferred from the balance sheet, not a disclosed segment build - Jungheinrich supplied no segment revenue detail in our inputs, and the split between the industrial business and the leasing arm is an estimate.

1. The industrial business - making, selling, servicing and renting forklifts and warehouse equipment. Normalised group operating margin of 7.25% on 5.5 billion euros of revenue gives about 400 million euros of operating profit. That sits between the 6.2% recorded in the first half of 2026 and the 8.2% of 2024, and slightly below the 7.7% consensus assumes from 2027 - I think the street's number is half a point generous. Removing an estimated 70 million euros from the leasing arm leaves 330 million of industrial operating profit. At 8.0 times enterprise value to operating profit, a mid-cycle multiple for a narrow-moat number-two European franchise with a recurring service and spare-parts stream: 2,640 million euros, or about 25.88 euros a share. This is 89% of the total value.

2. The captive leasing arm - the finance book that funds customer fleets. Estimated attributable equity of about 240 million euros, valued at 1.2 times: 290 million euros, or 2.84 euros a share. I value a lending book on its equity, never on an industrial earnings multiple.

3. Net cash overlay - 723 million euros of cash and short-term investments against 701 million of total debt at 30 June 2026: 22 million euros, or 0.21 euros a share. Small, and it describes the industrial company only; the leasing arm carries its own funding inside the other non-current liabilities. The 2025 dividend was already paid on 22 May 2026, so there is no pending distribution to add here.

Total: 2,952 million euros across 102 million shares = 28.94 euros. Cross-checks: 1.15 times the 25.06 euro book value, and 9.8 times the 2.96 euros consensus expects in 2027 - conservative against the 12.0 times implied by the 35.45 euro analyst consensus target, and against the 10-13 times this share traded at on 2024 earnings.
risk_reward: From 24.32 euros: the adverse case is 19.50 euros, the base-case fair value is 28.94 euros, and the favourable case is 39.50 euros. There is no structural floor to lean on - net cash is only 0.21 euros a share, there are no deal terms and no tender, and book value is an accounting number rather than a support level. The setup is close to symmetric to the base case, which is the core problem with buying it here: the distance down to the adverse case and the distance up to fair value are broadly similar, and only the favourable case offers real asymmetry. At 24.32 euros the discount to base-case fair value is well short of the entry bar this book requires, which is why the call is to wait rather than to buy.

peer_comps_note:
The peer file names the right comparison set - KION Group as the direct European rival, Toyota Industries as the global leader, plus Hyster-Yale and Mitsubishi Logisnext - and concludes Jungheinrich looks cheap against them, while noting that the gap versus KION is only partially explained by the current earnings trough and that KION's mix is more weighted toward higher-margin automation and software.

Two disciplines apply. First, the file supplied no live peer multiple to anchor on, so I quote none from memory; peer multiples de-rate, and citing a stale one would manufacture a discount that may not exist. My valuation is therefore anchored on Jungheinrich's own normalised earning power and its own trading history (10-13 times earnings on 2024 results), not on a borrowed peer multiple.

Second, and more important: the discount to KION is substantially shared-factor sector beta, not company-specific edge. Both names are riding exactly the same unresolved driver - the European industrial and warehouse capital-spending cycle - and both de-rated together through it. Crediting that gap as single-name alpha would be double-counting the cycle. What is genuinely company-specific here is narrower and cuts the other way: the open regulatory examination of the June 2025 accounts and the 45%-plus effective tax rate are Jungheinrich problems, not sector problems. Jungheinrich's own cross-checks are the useful ones: 0.97 times book value, about 3.6 times enterprise value to trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and roughly 8.2 times the 2.96 euros a share consensus expects in 2027.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Jungheinrich AG (JUN3.DE, XETRA preference share)

**Date of review:** 24 August 2026
**Price used throughout:** €24.32 per preference share (XETRA last close, 24 August 2026 tape; previous close €24.56, day range €24.26–24.56, 52-week range €21.72–38.16, 50-day average €24.34, 200-day average €29.37). Market value of all 102 million shares at that price: €2.48 billion. All figures in euros unless stated.

**Important disclosure about sources.** Jungheinrich does not publish an English-language earnings-call transcript through our licensed data provider — a search of that provider returned no transcript record for this listing at all. There is therefore **no transcript in front of me, and I quote none**. Sections that would normally rest on management's spoken words are instead built from the dated public disclosure record: the reported financial statements, the company's own financial calendar, the July 2026 forecast revision, the regulatory review opened in July 2026, and the movement of published analyst targets. Where I could not source something, I say so rather than filling the gap.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Jungheinrich has been telling for five years is a growth-and-mix story: a family-controlled German maker of forklift trucks and warehouse equipment, number two in Europe behind KION, using the e-commerce warehouse boom to push beyond selling machines into automation, software and services. Revenue backs the first half of that: €4.24 billion in 2021 rising to €5.55 billion in 2023, helped along by the 2023 purchase of the American warehouse-automation business Storage Solutions (roughly €330 million of cash out the door that year, the largest acquisition in the company's recent history).

Then the arc flattened. Revenue has now sat in the same place for three straight years — €5.55 billion in 2023, €5.39 billion in 2024, €5.50 billion in 2025 — and the emphasis in the reporting has quietly moved from expansion to holding the line. The company's own framing of last year, carried on its investor pages, is that it "ended financial year 2025 with an increase in incoming orders and revenue within a challenging economic environment." That sentence is doing a lot of work: it points the reader at the two metrics that went up and away from the one that collapsed.

Three dated events since July 2026 mark where the arc actually is now:

- **21 July 2026** — BaFin, the German financial regulator, opened an examination of Jungheinrich's financial statements as at 30 June 2025, connected to the planned disposal of the company's Russian business. The shares fell 2–3% on the day, to about €24.22.
- **23 July 2026** — the company adjusted its own 2026 forecast. The shares fell more than 5%. DZ Bank cut its fair-value estimate the same day from €43 to €35 while keeping a buy recommendation. I was **not able to retrieve a citable copy of the revised guidance figures themselves**, so I do not state them; I treat the revision as a downward one only because of the share-price reaction and the simultaneous target cut, and I flag that inference as an inference.
- **11 August 2026** — the half-year report to 30 June 2026 was published. Second-quarter order intake came in ahead of expectations, with the warehouse-equipment side beating; the shares finished roughly flat.

So the narrative has contracted from "structural growth into automation" to "the orders have turned, please look past the earnings." Whether that is fair is the whole question.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Because there is no transcript, I test the company's *positioning* — what its disclosure emphasises — against what the statements actually show.

| Claim implied by the disclosure | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Orders and revenue rose in 2025 | Revenue €5,502m vs €5,392m, up 2.0%. True, but it is 0.8% *below* 2023's €5,546m. Two years of standing still. | Technically true, materially thin |
| A "challenging economic environment" explains the year | Operating profit (EBIT) fell from €441m to €358m — a margin of 6.5% versus 8.2%. That is a real cyclical hit and the environment does explain most of it. | Fair |
| The environment explains the earnings collapse | It does not. Net profit fell from €289m to €104m, and earnings per share from €2.83 to €1.02 — down 64%. Operating profit fell only 19%. The gap is **€162m of charges booked below the operating line** (against €21m the prior year) plus a **47% effective tax rate** on €196m of pre-tax profit. Roughly two-thirds of the earnings collapse is one-offs and tax, not trading. | Diverges sharply — the headline is worse than the business |
| The business is holding its pricing | Gross margin 32.2% and stable. This is the single most important number in the file. If Jungheinrich were losing a competitive fight, it would show here first. It has not. | Confirmed |
| 2026 is a recovery year | First half 2026: revenue €2,669m against €2,657m a year earlier, up just 0.5%. Operating profit €166m against €211m, **down 21%**, a margin of 6.2% versus 7.9%. ## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: DETERIORATING**, with the first credible counter-evidence two weeks old.

Eighteen months of falling margins, a 64% earnings collapse, a mid-year guidance cut and an open regulatory examination is a deteriorating record by any reading. The order beat of 11 August 2026 is real and is the right leading indicator, but one quarter of orders does not reverse the classification — it starts the clock on reversing it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the cycle, and not the multiple. It is this: **roughly two-thirds of the earnings collapse came from charges and tax, not from trading — and the regulator has now opened a file on precisely those charges.** That cuts both ways, and the director must decide which way. If the charges are genuinely one-off, then normalised earnings power is far above the €1.02 the screen shows, and the stock at 0.97 times book with net cash is cheap. If the regulator finds the 30 June 2025 accounting was wrong, the restatement lands as an unscheduled headline into a stock that has already halved from €38, and the "one-off" framing goes with it. There is no way to handicap that outcome from public information, and no date by which it resolves.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is a combination of scale-cost (the number-two European position in a business where manufacturing and distribution density matter) and switching costs from the installed base — once a warehouse standardises on a fleet, the service contracts, spare parts and short-term rental revenue are sticky and recur. That is genuine, and the stable 32.2% gross margin is the evidence that it is holding. But it is narrow, not wide: the best operating margin this business has ever produced is around 8.5%, and return on invested capital is 5.8% today.

**Moat trend: ERODING** — on the returns evidence, which is what the standard requires. Operating margin has gone 8.2% (2024) → 6.5% (2025) → 6.2% (first half 2026), and return on invested capital has fallen with it. I record the trend as eroding while noting honestly that the stable gross margin argues this is operating-leverage and one-off damage rather than competitive damage. If the margin recovers toward 7.5% over the next four to six quarters, the correct label becomes stable.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** This is the part of the file that reads best. Warehouse automation is the structural force in material handling, and Jungheinrich is on the *right* side of it — it sells automated guided vehicles, warehouse robotics and racking, and it bought an American automation business specifically to be there. The shift of retail to e-commerce increases demand for warehouse equipment rather than destroying it. Electrification is a tailwind, not a threat, for a company that has led on lithium-ion trucks. There is no melting terminal value here. The cheapness is a cyclical fear-print on a narrow-moat industrial with an accounting cloud over it — **not a structurally shrinking base, and not a value trap in the terminal sense.** It may still be a value trap in the ordinary sense, which is to say cheap for another two years, but that is a timing problem, not an existence problem.

On 21 July 2026 BaFin opened an examination of the 30 June 2025 financial statements in connection with the Russian disposal - which is to say, an examination of exactly the charges the bull case needs to be genuinely one-off. There is no timetable, a finding of error must be published, and the outcome cannot be handicapped from public information. Two days later, on 23 July, the company cut its own 2026 forecast four months after setting it. That is a poor pair of facts to buy into at a 16% discount.

Or the regulator closing its file without a finding of error, which would remove the one risk in this name we cannot price. The most likely flush, and the one we would most like to buy into, is a dividend cut announced with the full-year results in late March 2027: the payout was 78% of earnings at the trough, it is not comfortably affordable on current earnings, and cutting it would push the yield-oriented German fund holders out mechanically at exactly the moment the operating recovery becomes visible.

The discount is real but modest, the business is durable but narrow-moated and currently earning single-digit returns on capital, and there are three separate forensic amber lights: an open regulatory file, an unexplained tax rate, and a flattered cash-flow line. That is not a profile that earns a large position. # Forensic Dossier — Jungheinrich AG (JUN3.DE, XETRA preference share)

**Date of review:** 24 August 2026
**Price used throughout:** €24.32 per preference share (XETRA last close, 24 August 2026 tape; previous close €24.56, day range €24.26–24.56, 52-week range €21.72–38.16, 50-day average €24.34, 200-day average €29.37). Market value of all 102 million shares at that price: €2.48 billion. All figures in euros unless stated.

**Important disclosure about sources.** Jungheinrich does not publish an English-language earnings-call transcript through our licensed data provider — a search of that provider returned no transcript record for this listing at all. There is therefore **no transcript in front of me, and I quote none**. Sections that would normally rest on management's spoken words are instead built from the dated public disclosure record: the reported financial statements, the company's own financial calendar, the July 2026 forecast revision, the regulatory review opened in July 2026, and the movement of published analyst targets. Where I could not source something, I say so rather than filling the gap.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Jungheinrich has been telling for five years is a growth-and-mix story: a family-controlled German maker of forklift trucks and warehouse equipment, number two in Europe behind KION, using the e-commerce warehouse boom to push beyond selling machines into automation, software and services. Revenue backs the first half of that: €4.24 billion in 2021 rising to €5.55 billion in 2023, helped along by the 2023 purchase of the American warehouse-automation business Storage Solutions (roughly €330 million of cash out the door that year, the largest acquisition in the company's recent history).

Then the arc flattened. Revenue has now sat in the same place for three straight years — €5.55 billion in 2023, €5.39 billion in 2024, €5.50 billion in 2025 — and the emphasis in the reporting has quietly moved from expansion to holding the line. The company's own framing of last year, carried on its investor pages, is that it "ended financial year 2025 with an increase in incoming orders and revenue within a challenging economic environment." That sentence is doing a lot of work: it points the reader at the two metrics that went up and away from the one that collapsed.

Three dated events since July 2026 mark where the arc actually is now:

- **21 July 2026** — BaFin, the German financial regulator, opened an examination of Jungheinrich's financial statements as at 30 June 2025, connected to the planned disposal of the company's Russian business. The shares fell 2–3% on the day, to about €24.22.
- **23 July 2026** — the company adjusted its own 2026 forecast. The shares fell more than 5%. DZ Bank cut its fair-value estimate the same day from €43 to €35 while keeping a buy recommendation. I was **not able to retrieve a citable copy of the revised guidance figures themselves**, so I do not state them; I treat the revision as a downward one only because of the share-price reaction and the simultaneous target cut, and I flag that inference as an inference.
- **11 August 2026** — the half-year report to 30 June 2026 was published. Second-quarter order intake came in ahead of expectations, with the warehouse-equipment side beating; the shares finished roughly flat.

So the narrative has contracted from "structural growth into automation" to "the orders have turned, please look past the earnings." Whether that is fair is the whole question.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Because there is no transcript, I test the company's *positioning* — what its disclosure emphasises — against what the statements actually show.

| Claim implied by the disclosure | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Orders and revenue rose in 2025 | Revenue €5,502m vs €5,392m, up 2.0%. True, but it is 0.8% *below* 2023's €5,546m. Two years of standing still. | Technically true, materially thin |
| A "challenging economic environment" explains the year | Operating profit (EBIT) fell from €441m to €358m — a margin of 6.5% versus 8.2%. That is a real cyclical hit and the environment does explain most of it. | Fair |
| The environment explains the earnings collapse | It does not. Net profit fell from €289m to €104m, and earnings per share from €2.83 to €1.02 — down 64%. Operating profit fell only 19%. The gap is **€162m of charges booked below the operating line** (against €21m the prior year) plus a **47% effective tax rate** on €196m of pre-tax profit. Roughly two-thirds of the earnings collapse is one-offs and tax, not trading. | Diverges sharply — the headline is worse than the business |
| The business is holding its pricing | Gross margin 32.2% and stable. This is the single most important number in the file. If Jungheinrich were losing a competitive fight, it would show here first. It has not. | Confirmed |
| 2026 is a recovery year | First half 2026: revenue €2,669m against €2,657m a year earlier, up just 0.5%. Operating profit €166m against €211m, **down 21%**, a margin of 6.2% versus 7.9%. Earnings per share €0.72 against €1.37, down 47%. The tax rate is still 44.6%. | Refuted so far — the second half of 2025 was not the bottom for margin |
| Free cash flow is strong | Reported free cash flow of €346m in 2025 looks superb against a €2.48bn market value. But capital expenditure of €145m is only **0.30 times** depreciation of €479m. A company cannot depreciate €479m of assets while replacing €145m of them. The missing spend is the short-term rental and lease fleet, which is not sitting in that capital-expenditure line. | Flattered — treat the 7.3x price-to-free-cash-flow screen and the 12% free-cash yield as artefacts, not facts |
| The balance sheet is conservative | At 30 June 2026: cash and short-term investments €723m against total debt €701m — **net cash of about €22m**, a genuine if small cushion. Shareholders' equity €2,556m, or €25.06 per share, so the stock trades at 0.97 times book. Share count unchanged at 102 million for six years: no dilution. | Confirmed, with a caveat below |

**The caveat on the balance sheet.** Jungheinrich runs a captive leasing arm. The €1,722m of long-term investments on the June 2026 balance sheet is substantially that lease book, and much of the €2,211m of other non-current liabilities is the funding behind it plus pensions. The tidy "net cash" figure describes the industrial company; it does not mean the group carries no financial leverage. Anyone treating €22m of net cash as a safety net is reading one line of a balance sheet that has two very different businesses inside it.

**The tax rate deserves its own paragraph.** Germany's statutory corporate rate is roughly 30%. Jungheinrich paid an effective 47% in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026. Two consecutive periods at that level is not noise. It is the signature of charges that are not deductible and losses in subsidiaries where the company cannot book a deferred tax asset. That is exactly what a Russian disposal would produce — and it is exactly the period, the 30 June 2025 accounts, that the regulator has now opened.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining, with a first sign of stabilisation.** No transcript exists for this name in our licensed source, so I cannot quote management or track their choice of words quarter by quarter, and I will not invent quotations. What the dated record shows instead:

- **Offensive posture through 2023**: a €330m acquisition, revenue pushed to a record.
- **Defensive posture from 2025**: the company's own summary of the year leads with orders and revenue — the two rising metrics — and does not lead with profit.
- **Retreat in July 2026**: cutting your own full-year forecast four months into the year, in the same week a regulator opens a file on your accounts, is the least confident act available to a management team. The market read it that way: down more than 5%.
- **First counter-evidence, 11 August 2026**: second-quarter orders beat, warehouse equipment beat. The shares did not rise, which tells you the market is no longer paying for order intake alone — it wants to see the margin.

The honest summary: confidence has been falling for eighteen months, and the first genuine piece of good news in that stretch landed two weeks ago and was ignored.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Low-to-Medium.**

The record is unambiguous on two points. First, the company cut its own 2026 forecast on 23 July 2026, having set it in late March 2026 — a four-month-old guide abandoned. Second, our screener's tracking shows the company has beaten expectations in only **2 of the last 5 quarters (40%)**, which is a below-average delivery rate and corroborates the cut rather than contradicting it.

There is no sandbagging pattern here — quite the opposite. A management team that sandbags produces a high beat rate and rising guidance; this one produces a 40% beat rate and a mid-year cut. The pattern is optimism at the start of the year followed by reality in the summer.

Against that, two things should be set on the credit side. The company has not diluted shareholders once in six years, and it maintained the dividend through the collapse (€80.5m paid in 2025 against €103.6m earned). Whether maintaining that dividend was discipline or stubbornness is section 6's problem.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a transcript I cannot report which questions management deflected. What I *can* report is where the published analyst view has moved, which is the same information one step removed:

- **19 May 2026** — Berenberg, buy, €37.
- **22 June and 24 July 2026** — Barclays, overweight, €39–40.
- **23 July 2026** — DZ Bank cuts fair value €43 → €35, keeps buy. The cut is 19%; the recommendation does not change.
- **14 August 2026** — Citi moves to buy with a €32 target, three days after the half-year report.
- **19 August 2026** — Bernstein raises its target to €47 and reiterates outperform.
- **Consensus**: about €35.45 across 11 analysts, with a buy rating overall — roughly 46% above the current price.

Two observations matter for a capital allocator. First, **the entire visible sell side is positive and has been through the whole decline**, which means there is no under-coverage edge in this name and no wall of scepticism left to convert. Second, and more interestingly, the direction of travel *since* the half-year report on 11 August is upward — Citi upgrading and Bernstein raising to €47 within eight days of the numbers. The analysts who have seen the half-year detail came away more constructive, not less. That is the strongest single piece of evidence that the order beat was real.

What nobody in the published record is visibly pressing on: the 45%-plus effective tax rate, and the gap between depreciation and capital expenditure. Those are the two questions I would want answered before sizing anything here.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **An open regulatory examination of the accounts.** BaFin opened a review of the 30 June 2025 statements on 21 July 2026, tied to the planned Russia disposal. Under German enforcement practice a finding of error must be published. There is no announced timetable. This is the single largest unquantifiable risk in the file, and it sits underneath the exact accounting — the disposal charges — that produced 2025's earnings collapse and the punitive tax rate.

🔴 **A mid-year forecast cut, 23 July 2026.** Four months after setting the guide.

🔴 **Margin still falling in 2026.** First-half operating margin of 6.2% is below 2025's full-year 6.5% and well below 2024's 8.2%. The trough has not been confirmed.

🔴 **Free cash flow is flattered.** Capital expenditure at 0.30 times depreciation means the headline free-cash-flow figure — and the cheap price-to-free-cash-flow multiple built on it — overstates what the business actually generates after keeping its rental fleet current.

🔴 **The dividend looks stretched.** €80.5m paid against €103.6m earned in 2025 is a 78% payout at a cyclical trough. On first-half 2026 earnings of €0.72 per share, holding the payout flat through 2026 would require paying out close to everything.

🔴 **Returns are weak in absolute terms.** Return on invested capital of 5.8% and return on equity of 11.5% are trough figures, but even the mid-cycle version of this business has never earned an operating margin above roughly 8.5%.

🟢 **Order intake beat in the second quarter of 2026**, reported 11 August, with warehouse equipment leading. This is the leading indicator and it turned first, as it should.

🟢 **Gross margin has not moved.** 32.2% and stable. The competitive position is intact; the damage is operating leverage on flat revenue plus one-offs, not price.

🟢 **Revenue has not shrunk.** Flat at around €5.5 billion for three years through a genuinely poor European industrial cycle.

🟢 **No dilution and a clean industrial balance sheet.** 102 million shares for six years; cash and short-term investments modestly exceed total debt. There is no maturity wall and no refinancing risk in the next three to nine months.

🟢 **The sell side got more positive after seeing the half-year detail**, not less (Citi upgrade 14 August, Bernstein target raise 19 August).

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The tax rate is the loudest quiet signal in the file.** A 47% effective rate in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026, against a ~30% statutory rate, says there are losses somewhere in the group that cannot be sheltered and charges that cannot be deducted. That wedge matters enormously to anyone underwriting a recovery: even if operating profit returns to €440m, a 45% tax rate rather than a normal 30% costs roughly €0.60 of earnings per share. **Operating recovery and earnings recovery are not the same event here, and the market's forward multiple assumes they are.**

**The regulator's file and the tax rate point at the same thing.** Both trace back to the Russian disposal and how it was accounted for at 30 June 2025. That is not a coincidence to be waved away; it is one issue showing up in two places.

**The share structure is a silent veto.** The listed instrument is the non-voting preference share. The ordinary shares are held by the founding family and are not listed. Whatever the sum-of-the-parts arithmetic says, **no activist can force a break-up, a sale, a buyback or a board change here.** Every classic special-situation lever — governance reset, strategic review under pressure, premium takeout — is structurally unavailable. Any thesis that quietly relies on "someone will do something about this discount" is unsupported.

**Goodwill appears to move on the balance sheet between December 2025 (€377m) and June 2026 (nil), while other intangibles rise from €262m to €663m.** The combined total barely changes, so this reads as a reclassification in the data feed rather than a write-off. I flag it because it is the kind of movement that deserves a direct look at the primary filing before anyone sizes a position, and I could not obtain that filing.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: DETERIORATING**, with the first credible counter-evidence two weeks old.

Eighteen months of falling margins, a 64% earnings collapse, a mid-year guidance cut and an open regulatory examination is a deteriorating record by any reading. The order beat of 11 August 2026 is real and is the right leading indicator, but one quarter of orders does not reverse the classification — it starts the clock on reversing it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the cycle, and not the multiple. It is this: **roughly two-thirds of the earnings collapse came from charges and tax, not from trading — and the regulator has now opened a file on precisely those charges.** That cuts both ways, and the director must decide which way. If the charges are genuinely one-off, then normalised earnings power is far above the €1.02 the screen shows, and the stock at 0.97 times book with net cash is cheap. If the regulator finds the 30 June 2025 accounting was wrong, the restatement lands as an unscheduled headline into a stock that has already halved from €38, and the "one-off" framing goes with it. There is no way to handicap that outcome from public information, and no date by which it resolves.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is a combination of scale-cost (the number-two European position in a business where manufacturing and distribution density matter) and switching costs from the installed base — once a warehouse standardises on a fleet, the service contracts, spare parts and short-term rental revenue are sticky and recur. That is genuine, and the stable 32.2% gross margin is the evidence that it is holding. But it is narrow, not wide: the best operating margin this business has ever produced is around 8.5%, and return on invested capital is 5.8% today.

**Moat trend: ERODING** — on the returns evidence, which is what the standard requires. Operating margin has gone 8.2% (2024) → 6.5% (2025) → 6.2% (first half 2026), and return on invested capital has fallen with it. I record the trend as eroding while noting honestly that the stable gross margin argues this is operating-leverage and one-off damage rather than competitive damage. If the margin recovers toward 7.5% over the next four to six quarters, the correct label becomes stable.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** This is the part of the file that reads best. Warehouse automation is the structural force in material handling, and Jungheinrich is on the *right* side of it — it sells automated guided vehicles, warehouse robotics and racking, and it bought an American automation business specifically to be there. The shift of retail to e-commerce increases demand for warehouse equipment rather than destroying it. Electrification is a tailwind, not a threat, for a company that has led on lithium-ion trucks. There is no melting terminal value here. The cheapness is a cyclical fear-print on a narrow-moat industrial with an accounting cloud over it — **not a structurally shrinking base, and not a value trap in the terminal sense.** It may still be a value trap in the ordinary sense, which is to say cheap for another two years, but that is a timing problem, not an existence problem.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory weakening · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

This is not a sandbagging management team whose guidance can be trusted as a floor; it is one that has been too optimistic and had to retreat.

Fifth, the effective tax rate is a structural wedge between an operating recovery and an earnings recovery. At 47% in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026 against a German statutory rate near 30%, the arithmetic says there are losses in the group that cannot be sheltered. Even if operating profit returns fully to 440 million euros, a 45% tax rate rather than a normal 30% costs roughly 0.60 euros of earnings per share. Consensus earnings of 2.96 euros for 2027 implicitly assume this normalises. If it does not, the forward multiple people think they are paying is meaningfully wrong.

Sixth, this is not a high-return business even at the top of its cycle. The best operating margin Jungheinrich has ever produced is around 8.5%. Return on invested capital today is 5.8% and return on equity 11.5%. A narrow-moat industrial that earns single-digit returns on capital does not deserve a premium multiple, and at 0.97 times book with a mid-cycle recovery already the consensus base case, it is not obviously getting a discount either.

Seventh, there is no lever. The listed instrument is the non-voting preference share; the ordinary shares are held by the founding family and are not listed. No activist can force a break-up, a buyback, a sale or a board change. Every classic special-situation escape route is structurally closed. The only thing that fixes this stock is the company earning its way out, on its own timetable.

Finally, the dividend looks stretched. The company paid 80.5 million euros against 103.6 million of earnings in 2025 - a 78% payout at a cyclical trough - and first-half 2026 earnings of 0.72 euros a share do not comfortably support holding it flat. A cut announced with the full-year results in late March 2027 would be the correct capital-allocation decision and would still force German income-oriented funds to sell mechanically.

Our call is to wait for a better price rather than buy here, at a moderate level of conviction, and to say plainly what we are waiting for.

The business case is more interesting than the screen suggests, and it is more interesting than the headline earnings collapse suggests. Jungheinrich's earnings per share fell 64% last year, from 2.83 euros to 1.02, but operating profit fell only 19%. Roughly two-thirds of that collapse came from about 162 million euros of charges booked below the operating line and an effective tax rate of 47%, both traceable to the planned disposal of the Russian business. Meanwhile gross margin has not moved at all - 32.2% and stable - which is the evidence that matters most, because a company losing a competitive fight loses it in gross margin first. Revenue has been flat rather than shrinking for three years through a poor European cycle, the balance sheet carries a small net cash position with no maturity wall, the share count has been unchanged for six years, and second-quarter order intake beat expectations in the half-year report published on 11 August 2026. This is a cyclically compressed, narrow-moat industrial - not a melting franchise. On the structural question the file reads well: warehouse automation is the force reshaping this industry and Jungheinrich sells into it rather than being displaced by it, e-commerce raises demand for warehouse equipment, and electrification is a tailwind for a company that led on lithium-ion trucks. The cheapness is a fear print, not a terminal decline.

Three things stop us buying it today.

The first is arithmetic. Our base-case sum-of-the-parts fair value is 28.94 euros a share, built from a normalised 7.25% operating margin on the industrial business at eight times operating profit, the captive leasing book at a modest premium to its estimated equity, and a small net cash overlay. Against a 24.32 euro price, that is a discount well short of what this book requires to commit capital, and the adverse case at 19.50 euros is almost exactly as far below the price as fair value is above it. Symmetric is not good enough.

The second is a correction to the reason most screens like this stock. It shows 7.3 times price to free cash flow and a 12% free-cash yield, but capital expenditure is running at 0.30 times depreciation - 145 million euros against 479 million. The short-term rental and lease fleet spend is not in that line. The cash-flow cheapness is a classification artefact, and correcting it is why our fair value sits below the 35.45 euro analyst consensus rather than above it. We also part company with consensus on tax: two consecutive periods at a 45%-plus effective rate against a 30% statutory rate is structural until proven otherwise, and it drives a wedge of roughly 0.60 euros a share between an operating recovery and an earnings recovery that the street's 2.96 euro 2027 estimate does not appear to carry.

The third is the regulator. On 21 July 2026 BaFin opened an examination of the 30 June 2025 financial statements in connection with the Russian disposal - which is to say, an examination of exactly the charges the bull case needs to be genuinely one-off. There is no timetable, a finding of error must be published, and the outcome cannot be handicapped from public information. Two days later, on 23 July, the company cut its own 2026 forecast four months after setting it. That is a poor pair of facts to buy into at a 16% discount.

We also note what this name does not offer. Eleven analysts cover it and every one is positive, so there is no coverage edge. The listed shares are non-voting preference shares with the ordinary shares held by the founding family, so no activist can force anything and no takeover premium exists - the usual deep-value escape hatches are structurally closed. And the discount to KION is largely the same European industrial capital-spending cycle both companies are riding, which makes it shared sector movement rather than company-specific edge; crediting it as edge would be double-counting.

So: what would change the call. Any one of three things. A price at or below 21.50 euros - through the 21.72 euro 52-week low - which would widen the discount to our fair value past 25% and clear the entry bar on the arithmetic alone. Or a nine-month operating margin back above 7.0% in the statement due 10 November 2026, confirming the first half was the trough and that the order beat is converting. Or the regulator closing its file without a finding of error, which would remove the one risk in this name we cannot price. The most likely flush, and the one we would most like to buy into, is a dividend cut announced with the full-year results in late March 2027: the payout was 78% of earnings at the trough, it is not comfortably affordable on current earnings, and cutting it would push the yield-oriented German fund holders out mechanically at exactly the moment the operating recovery becomes visible.

On the value case judged on its own - price against our fair value and the quality of the numbers, setting aside timing entirely - we rate it moderate. The discount is real but modest, the business is durable but narrow-moated and currently earning single-digit returns on capital, and there are three separate forensic amber lights: an open regulatory file, an unexplained tax rate, and a flattered cash-flow line. That is not a profile that earns a large position. It is a good name to own considerably lower, and the calendar gives us two dated chances - November and late March - to find out whether we will get it there.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Jungheinrich AG (JUN3.DE, XETRA preference share)

**Date of review:** 24 August 2026
**Price used throughout:** €24.32 per preference share (XETRA last close, 24 August 2026 tape; previous close €24.56, day range €24.26–24.56, 52-week range €21.72–38.16, 50-day average €24.34, 200-day average €29.37). Market value of all 102 million shares at that price: €2.48 billion. All figures in euros unless stated.

**Important disclosure about sources.** Jungheinrich does not publish an English-language earnings-call transcript through our licensed data provider — a search of that provider returned no transcript record for this listing at all. There is therefore **no transcript in front of me, and I quote none**. Sections that would normally rest on management's spoken words are instead built from the dated public disclosure record: the reported financial statements, the company's own financial calendar, the July 2026 forecast revision, the regulatory review opened in July 2026, and the movement of published analyst targets. Where I could not source something, I say so rather than filling the gap.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Jungheinrich has been telling for five years is a growth-and-mix story: a family-controlled German maker of forklift trucks and warehouse equipment, number two in Europe behind KION, using the e-commerce warehouse boom to push beyond selling machines into automation, software and services. Revenue backs the first half of that: €4.24 billion in 2021 rising to €5.55 billion in 2023, helped along by the 2023 purchase of the American warehouse-automation business Storage Solutions (roughly €330 million of cash out the door that year, the largest acquisition in the company's recent history).

Then the arc flattened. Revenue has now sat in the same place for three straight years — €5.55 billion in 2023, €5.39 billion in 2024, €5.50 billion in 2025 — and the emphasis in the reporting has quietly moved from expansion to holding the line. The company's own framing of last year, carried on its investor pages, is that it "ended financial year 2025 with an increase in incoming orders and revenue within a challenging economic environment." That sentence is doing a lot of work: it points the reader at the two metrics that went up and away from the one that collapsed.

Three dated events since July 2026 mark where the arc actually is now:

- **21 July 2026** — BaFin, the German financial regulator, opened an examination of Jungheinrich's financial statements as at 30 June 2025, connected to the planned disposal of the company's Russian business. The shares fell 2–3% on the day, to about €24.22.
- **23 July 2026** — the company adjusted its own 2026 forecast. The shares fell more than 5%. DZ Bank cut its fair-value estimate the same day from €43 to €35 while keeping a buy recommendation. I was **not able to retrieve a citable copy of the revised guidance figures themselves**, so I do not state them; I treat the revision as a downward one only because of the share-price reaction and the simultaneous target cut, and I flag that inference as an inference.
- **11 August 2026** — the half-year report to 30 June 2026 was published. Second-quarter order intake came in ahead of expectations, with the warehouse-equipment side beating; the shares finished roughly flat.

So the narrative has contracted from "structural growth into automation" to "the orders have turned, please look past the earnings." Whether that is fair is the whole question.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Because there is no transcript, I test the company's *positioning* — what its disclosure emphasises — against what the statements actually show.

| Claim implied by the disclosure | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Orders and revenue rose in 2025 | Revenue €5,502m vs €5,392m, up 2.0%. True, but it is 0.8% *below* 2023's €5,546m. Two years of standing still. | Technically true, materially thin |
| A "challenging economic environment" explains the year | Operating profit (EBIT) fell from €441m to €358m — a margin of 6.5% versus 8.2%. That is a real cyclical hit and the environment does explain most of it. | Fair |
| The environment explains the earnings collapse | It does not. Net profit fell from €289m to €104m, and earnings per share from €2.83 to €1.02 — down 64%. Operating profit fell only 19%. The gap is **€162m of charges booked below the operating line** (against €21m the prior year) plus a **47% effective tax rate** on €196m of pre-tax profit. Roughly two-thirds of the earnings collapse is one-offs and tax, not trading. | Diverges sharply — the headline is worse than the business |
| The business is holding its pricing | Gross margin 32.2% and stable. This is the single most important number in the file. If Jungheinrich were losing a competitive fight, it would show here first. It has not. | Confirmed |
| 2026 is a recovery year | First half 2026: revenue €2,669m against €2,657m a year earlier, up just 0.5%. Operating profit €166m against €211m, **down 21%**, a margin of 6.2% versus 7.9%. Earnings per share €0.72 against €1.37, down 47%. The tax rate is still 44.6%. | Refuted so far — the second half of 2025 was not the bottom for margin |
| Free cash flow is strong | Reported free cash flow of €346m in 2025 looks superb against a €2.48bn market value. But capital expenditure of €145m is only **0.30 times** depreciation of €479m. A company cannot depreciate €479m of assets while replacing €145m of them. The missing spend is the short-term rental and lease fleet, which is not sitting in that capital-expenditure line. | Flattered — treat the 7.3x price-to-free-cash-flow screen and the 12% free-cash yield as artefacts, not facts |
| The balance sheet is conservative | At 30 June 2026: cash and short-term investments €723m against total debt €701m — **net cash of about €22m**, a genuine if small cushion. Shareholders' equity €2,556m, or €25.06 per share, so the stock trades at 0.97 times book. Share count unchanged at 102 million for six years: no dilution. | Confirmed, with a caveat below |

**The caveat on the balance sheet.** Jungheinrich runs a captive leasing arm. The €1,722m of long-term investments on the June 2026 balance sheet is substantially that lease book, and much of the €2,211m of other non-current liabilities is the funding behind it plus pensions. The tidy "net cash" figure describes the industrial company; it does not mean the group carries no financial leverage. Anyone treating €22m of net cash as a safety net is reading one line of a balance sheet that has two very different businesses inside it.

**The tax rate deserves its own paragraph.** Germany's statutory corporate rate is roughly 30%. Jungheinrich paid an effective 47% in 2025 and 44.6% in the first half of 2026. Two consecutive periods at that level is not noise. It is the signature of charges that are not deductible and losses in subsidiaries where the company cannot book a deferred tax asset. That is exactly what a Russian disposal would produce — and it is exactly the period, the 30 June 2025 accounts, that the regulator has now opened.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining, with a first sign of stabilisation.** No transcript exists for this name in our licensed source, so I cannot quote management or track their choice of words quarter by quarter, and I will not invent quotations. What the dated record shows instead:

- **Offensive posture through 2023**: a €330m acquisition, revenue pushed to a record.
- **Defensive posture from 2025**: the company's own summary of the year leads with orders and revenue — the two rising metrics — and does not lead with profit.
- **Retreat in July 2026**: cutting your own full-year forecast four months into the year, in the same week a regulator opens a file on your accounts, is the least confident act available to a management team. The market read it that way: down more than 5%.
- **First counter-evidence, 11 August 2026**: second-quarter orders beat, warehouse equipment beat. The shares did not rise, which tells you the market is no longer paying for order intake alone — it wants to see the margin.

The honest summary: confidence has been falling for eighteen months, and the first genuine piece of good news in that stretch landed two weeks ago and was ignored.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Low-to-Medium.**

The record is unambiguous on two points. First, the company cut its own 2026 forecast on 23 July 2026, having set it in late March 2026 — a four-month-old guide abandoned. Second, our screener's tracking shows the company has beaten expectations in only **2 of the last 5 quarters (40%)**, which is a below-average delivery rate and corroborates the cut rather than contradicting it.

There is no sandbagging pattern here — quite the opposite. A management team that sandbags produces a high beat rate and rising guidance; this one produces a 40% beat rate and a mid-year cut. The pattern is optimism at the start of the year followed by reality in the summer.

Against that, two things should be set on the credit side. The company has not diluted shareholders once in six years, and it maintained the dividend through the collapse (€80.5m paid in 2025 against €103.6m earned). Whether maintaining that dividend was discipline or stubbornness is section 6's problem.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a transcript I cannot report which questions management deflected. What I *can* report is where the published analyst view has moved, which is the same information one step removed:

- **19 May 2026** — Berenberg, buy, €37.
- **22 June and 24 July 2026** — Barclays, overweight, €39–40.
- **23 July 2026** — DZ Bank cuts fair value €43 → €35, keeps buy. The cut is 19%; the recommendation does not change.
- **14 August 2026** — Citi moves to buy with a €32 target, three days after the half-year report.
- **19 August 2026** — Bernstein raises its target to €47 and reiterates outperform.
- **Consensus**: about €35.45 across 11 analysts, with a buy rating overall — roughly 46% above the current price.

Two observations matter for a capital allocator. First, **the entire visible sell side is positive and has been through the whole decline**, which means there is no under-coverage edge in this name and no wall of scepticism left to convert. Second, and more interestingly, the direction of travel *since* the half-year report on 11 August is upward — Citi upgrading and Bernstein raising to €47 within eight days of the numbers. The analysts who have seen the half-year detail came away more constructive, not less. That is the strongest single piece of evidence that the order beat was real.

What nobody in the published record is visibly pressing on: the 45%-plus effective tax rate, and the gap between depreciation and capital expenditure. Those are the two questions I would want answered before sizing anything here.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **An open regulatory examination of the accounts.** BaFin opened a review of the 30 June 2025 statements on 21 July 2026, tied to the planned Russia disposal. Under German enforcement practice a finding of error must be published. There is no announced timetable. This is the single largest unquantifiable risk in the file, and it sits underneath the exact accounting — the disposal charges — that produced 2025's earnings collapse and the punitive tax rate.

🔴 **A mid-year forecast cut, 23 July 2026.** Four months after setting the guide.

🔴 **Margin still falling in 2026.** First-half operating margin of 6.2% is below 2025's full-year 6.5% and well below 2024's 8.2%. The trough has not been confirmed.

🔴 **Free cash flow is flattered.** Capital expenditure at 0.30 times depreciation means the headline free-cash-flow figure — and the cheap price-to-free-cash-flow multiple built on it — overstates what the business actually generates after keeping its rental fleet current.

🔴 **The dividend looks stretched.** €80.5m paid against €103.6m earned in 2025 is a 78% payout at a cyclical trough. On first-half 2026 earnings of €0.72 per share, holding the payout flat through 2026 would require paying out close to everything.

🔴 **Returns are weak in absolute terms.** Return on invested capital of 5.8% and return on equity of 11.5% are trough figures, but even the mid-cycle version of this business has never earned an operating margin above roughly 8.5%.

🟢 **Order intake beat in the second quarter of 2026**, reported 11 August, with warehouse equipment leading. This is the leading indicator and it turned first, as it should.

🟢 **Gross margin has not moved.** 32.2% and stable. The competitive position is intact; the damage is operating leverage on flat revenue plus one-offs, not price.

🟢 **Revenue has not shrunk.** Flat at around €5.5 billion for three years through a genuinely poor European industrial cycle.

🟢 **No dilution and a clean industrial balance sheet.** 102 million shares for six years; cash and short-term investments modestly exceed total debt. There is no maturity wall and no refinancing risk in the next three to nine months.

🟢 **The sell side got more positive after seeing the half-year detail**, not less (Citi upgrade 14 August, Bernstein target raise 19 August).
